t: Apply Operations on Array to Maximize Sum of Squares — Bit-Pooling Greedy
o: The AND/OR swap operation lets bits migrate freely between elements: applying it to pairs sorts bits so that each bit position's total count across the array is invariant, and any distribution of those bit counts into k numbers is achievable. So the problem reduces to: given cnt[b] = how many numbers have bit b set, split these bits into k numbers maximizing the sum of squares. Constraints (n ≤ 1e5, values < 2^30) point to a per-bit counting solution rather than any simulation.
k: The operation preserves, for every bit position, the number of array elements containing that bit — and any redistribution is reachable.
Sum of squares is maximized by making the chosen numbers as unequal as possible: greedily give each new number the highest available bits first.

a.i: Count occurrences of each bit. Build the k picked numbers one at a time: for each number, scan bits from high to low and take a bit whenever its count is still positive, decrementing the count. Taking a high bit into the current number always beats saving it, by an exchange argument on convexity of x^2.
s: Compute cnt[b] for b = 0..30 over all nums.
Repeat k times: form x by setting bit b (high to low) whenever cnt[b] > 0, decrementing counts.
Add x*x modulo 1e9+7 to the answer.
a.t: O(31 * (n + k)) — one pass to count bits, then k extractions of at most 31 bits
a.sp: O(1) extra — a fixed-size count array

w: This greedy is the intended solution; prove correctness via the exchange argument (moving a higher bit into a larger number never decreases the sum of squares). Pitfalls: overflowing 64-bit when squaring (x < 2^31 fits in long long but reduce mod first or use unsigned care), and remembering the modulus applies to the squares, not the bit counts. Follow-up: maximize sum of products of pairs instead — the greedy changes.
